trace.msg: Let's look at this puzzle carefully. I'll only move when I can explain why.
Going left would leave number 2 unreachable without crossing a higher number; going right, the next 2 moves are forced and the line gets stuck at cell (6,7). So the line goes up.
Number 2 is only reachable this way.
Cell (7,6) has only two exits, so the line must pass through it now: it goes down.
Only one free cell next to the line, so it goes right.
Going left would force the line onto number 4 before its turn. So the line goes up.
Going up, the next 3 moves are forced and the line gets stuck at cell (1,5). So the line goes left.
Going left would leave number 4 unreachable without crossing a higher number. So the line goes down.
Number 4 is next and right here, so the line takes it.
I can't rule out up or left yet, so I'll make an educated guess: up.

Contradiction! Every way forward fails: going up, every way of continuing runs into a dead end within a few moves; going left, every way of continuing runs into a dead end within a few moves. So my guess (up from number 5) was wrong, so the line must go left.
Number 6 is only reachable this way.
The line must go left: down is number 8, which comes later.
Going down would force the line onto number 8 before its turn; going left, the next move is forced and the line gets stuck at cell (4,2). So the line goes up.
Going up would leave number 8 unreachable without crossing a higher number. So the line goes left.
Going left would cut off the bottom-left corner (10 cells). So the line goes down.
Going left would cut off the bottom-left corner (8 cells). So the line goes down.
Going down would cut off the bottom edge (4 cells). So the line goes right.
Going down would leave both cell (7,2) and cell (7,4) needing the line next, and it can't do both. So the line goes right.
Only one free cell next to the line, so it goes down.
Going down would force the line onto number 13 before its turn. So the line goes right.

Going right would strand number 11: it would be left with only one free neighbour; going down would leave both cell (3,3) and cell (3,5) needing the line next, and it can't do both. So the line goes up.
Only one free cell next to the line, so it goes right.
Going down would cut off the top-right corner (4 cells). So the line goes right.
Cell (1,7) has only two exits, so the line must pass through it now: it goes right.
Only one free cell next to the line, so it goes down.
Every cell is covered and the numbers are in order. Case closed!
